```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%", dpi = 160)
library(behavSSF)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_ssf())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(bg = "white"))
library(patchwork)
source(system.file("extdata", "zebra-state-comparison.R", package = "behavSSF", mustWork = TRUE))
comparison <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "zebra-state-comparison.rds",
  package = "behavSSF", mustWork = TRUE))
theme_set(theme_ssf())
```

Does a third state tell us more about the zebra's movement? We compare one
to four states on the Hwange track, using labels and rules that we define
ourselves. The [first zebra vignette](zebra-hwange.html) applies the taxonomy
from Bouderbala, Nicosia and Fortin (2026). Here we ask a different question
about short, intermediate and long steps, with vegetation in the model.

We keep three decisions separate. Did the model fit reliably? Does it
satisfy our state definitions? Does it predict reserved observations better?
A good predictive score does not settle the ecological interpretation.

The figures below use a saved run shipped with the package. The code to
refit it is shown explicitly. Rendering this vignette reads the saved fits
rather than repeating the full optimisation.

The full comparison takes about 27 minutes with six workers on the reference
macOS machine. Other machines and optimisation outcomes can take longer.

## Prepare the same observations and alternatives

The helper reconstructs the choice sets from the archived vegetation grid.
It retains 6,375 half-hour steps in 26 segments and draws 128 controls per
step from a mixture of gamma and log-normal lengths with uniform turns.
It discards 565 proposed controls outside the vegetation map. Every candidate
receives the same remaining alternatives. The weights retain the raw mixture
density. Conditioning on staying inside the map would multiply all weights
within a step by the same factor. That factor cancels from the conditional
choice probabilities used here. We do not use these proportional weights
to report an absolute physical normaliser.
The nearest grassland target is fixed at the beginning of each step.

```{r prepare, eval=FALSE}
library(behavSSF)
source(system.file("extdata", "zebra-state-comparison.R",
  package = "behavSSF", mustWork = TRUE))
choices <- zebra_state_data(seed = 660301L, n_controls = 128L)
blocks <- ssf_blocks(choices, n_blocks = 3L)
```

`ssf_blocks()` places chronological cuts near thirds of the track, while
keeping each uninterrupted segment whole. Each block is reserved once.
The other two blocks supply the training data, including all starting values.

```{r block-table, echo=FALSE}
obs <- comparison$observations
block_id <- unname(comparison$blocks[as.character(obs$ID)])
knitr::kable(data.frame(Block = 1:3,
  Steps = as.integer(table(block_id)),
  Segments = vapply(1:3, function(b) length(unique(obs$ID[block_id == b])), integer(1))))
```

These blocks belong to one animal. They assess prediction on this track,
not transfer to a new animal. Whole segments are treated as independent
runs. This split trains on both earlier and later segments; it is not a
forecast made using past observations alone.

## Write down what the labels mean

A taxonomy supplies the labels, an ordering and optional rules. The number
of labels sets the number of fitted states. Here the labels follow increasing
intrinsic mean step length. For two or more states, we require the largest
mean to exceed twice the smallest. That factor is our definition of a useful
length contrast, not a behavioural threshold learned by the package.

```{r taxonomies}
selection <- ~ cos_angle + cos_diff_theta_to_target + habitat

length_taxonomy <- function(labels) {
  force(labels)
  ssf_taxonomy(
    name = paste0("length_", length(labels)),
    labels = labels,
    formula = selection,
    order_by = "mean_step",
    rules = if (length(labels) > 1L) function(s) {
      first <- labels[1L]
      last <- labels[length(labels)]
      c(length_ratio = s$metrics[last, "mean_step"] >
          2 * s$metrics[first, "mean_step"])
    }
  )
}

taxonomies <- lapply(list(
  "All steps",
  c("Short", "Long"),
  c("Short", "Intermediate", "Long"),
  c("Shortest", "Short-middle", "Long-middle", "Longest")
), length_taxonomy)
```

Always address a state by its label inside a rule. For example,
`s$metrics["Long", "mean_step"]` finds the long state even if the optimiser
calls it state 1. The rows are not sorted by length. A rule must return a
named logical vector. `FALSE` or `NA` fails the corresponding check.

With `step_family`, the formula contains the angular and selection terms.
The package supplies the radial distribution separately. It therefore does
not include `step` or `log_step` in this formula.

## Fit all candidates and reserve each block in turn

```{r refit, eval=FALSE}
comparison <- compare_ssf_states(
  choices, taxonomies, blocks = blocks,
  step_families = c("gamma", "weibull"),
  initializers = zebra_state_initializers_extended,
  normalization = "importance", short_iter = 100L,
  long_iter = 950L, seed = 61001L, workers = 1L,
  score_failed_hessian = TRUE
)
comparison
summary(comparison)$block_scores
```

For this run, `zebra_state_initializers_extended()` supplies a movement-only fit
and a start based on groups of observed lengths. Both are calculated again
inside each training split. The one-state model uses one start. Four-state fits also use training-only perturbations of the two anchors: eight starts for full-track
fits and four for each held-out training job. For another
study, omit `initializers` and set `n_starts`, or supply a function using
training rows only. Choose the start by training likelihood, never by the
reserved score.

The strict screen requires convergence, a positive Hessian, a maximum
absolute curvature-scaled gradient no larger than 0.01, agreement between the objective and
forward calculation within 1e-7, and valid movement parameters. The taxonomy
is then assessed on the retained full-track fit. Its default checks also
cover occupancy and self-transition probabilities.

```{r candidate-table, echo=FALSE}
candidates <- comparison$candidates
candidates$gain <- NA_real_
for (f in unique(candidates$family)) {
  use <- candidates$family == f
  baseline <- candidates$mean_log_score[use & candidates$states == 2L]
  candidates$gain[use] <- candidates$mean_log_score[use] - baseline
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Family = candidates$family, States = candidates$states,
  `Numerical checks` = candidates$numerical_passed,
  `Taxonomy passed` = candidates$taxonomy_passed,
  `Blocks scored` = paste0(candidates$blocks_scored, "/3"),
  `Gain over two states` = round(candidates$gain, 3), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Strict held-out log-score gains per step, relative to two states of the same family. Missing values mean incomplete block coverage.")
```

The score integrates over the hidden states. It is the log probability
of the observed endpoint among its alternatives, not the proportion of
correct behavioural labels. Larger scores predict the reserved endpoints
better. The pooled score weights every step equally and requires all three
blocks. `comparison$starts` retains every attempt and its failure reason.

```{r scores, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt="Held-out score gains for one to four states, with separate gamma and Weibull panels and one point per reserved block."}
plot(comparison, reference = "gamma::length_2") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(length_1 = "#82949d", length_2 = "#193541",
    length_3 = "#147b80", length_4 = "#be6d3d"),
    labels = c(length_1 = "One state", length_2 = "Two states",
      length_3 = "Three states", length_4 = "Four states")) +
  labs(title = "More states can improve endpoint prediction",
    subtitle = "Both panels use the two-state gamma fit as their reference",
    colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The full-track AIC favours four states in both families. Three states improve
on two in every reserved block, with pooled gains of 0.042 and 0.041 nats per
step for gamma and Weibull. The regular gamma four-state fits improve on three
in every block, by a further 0.0176 nats per step when pooled. The Weibull
four-state model has no pooled score because one training block has no
numerically eligible fit at this restart budget.

Both full-track four-state fits fail the default taxonomy on occupancy alone.
The rarest states contain 318 gamma steps and 317 Weibull steps. A 5% cutoff
requires at least 319 of these 6,375 steps. That is a difference of only one
or two steps, not evidence that a fourth state does not exist.

```{r occupancy-policy}
occupancy_policy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("gamma", "weibull"), function(family) {
  fit <- comparison$fits[[paste0(family, "::length_4")]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c(.04, .05), function(threshold) {
    a <- assess_taxonomy(fit, taxonomies[[4]], "area", min_occupancy = threshold)
    data.frame(Family = family, Minimum = threshold,
      Smallest_state = min(tabulate(fit$state, nbins = 4L)), Accepted = a$accepted)
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(occupancy_policy)
```

At 4%, both full-track taxonomies pass without changing the fitted model.
This is a sensitivity check chosen after seeing the result. It is not a
recommendation to lower the cutoff until a preferred answer passes. Decide
what occupancy is useful for the ecological question, and report that policy
along with prediction and numerical stability.

The table separates fit reliability, the taxonomy decision and prediction.
Read all three columns before choosing a state count. A higher score can come
from a model whose uncertainty or proposed labels are poorly supported.

```{r four-state-checks, echo=FALSE}
four <- subset(comparison$candidates, states == 4L)
knitr::kable(four[c("family", "numerical_passed", "taxonomy_passed",
  "blocks_scored", "mean_log_score", "point_mean_log_score")], digits = 4,
  caption = "Four-state results. Strict scores require every reserved block.")
```

The main replication attempts eight separate fits for each full-track four-state
fit and four for each held-out training fit, using training-only anchors
and perturbations. The
sensitivity tables record the relative smallest curvature eigenvalue, its
condition number and the smallest decoded occupancy for every start. The four
highest likelihood full-track starts per family are inspected through their saved
state profiles. Their labels are aligned by mean length. Similar likelihoods
do not by themselves establish stable state coefficients. If nearly equal
likelihoods come with very different profiles, the labels are not settled.
Look for a stable pattern that also meets the ecological rules you wrote.

`score_failed_hessian = TRUE` adds a separate point-prediction sensitivity
analysis. Convergence, the scaled score, objective agreement and kernel
validity still apply, but the Hessian screen can fail. Those scores remain
in `point_mean_log_score`; they never replace the strict scores. A failed
curvature check means the usual coefficient intervals are unavailable. It
can reflect difficult optimisation or weak identification. This diagnostic
alone cannot establish which explanation is responsible.

Five of the forty four-state attempts return errors: four movement-anchor
starts contain zero transition probabilities, and one produces nonfinite
emissions. Sixteen more do not yield a Hessian that can be scaled. These
outcomes remain in `comparison$starts`; they are not counted as successful
optimisations. The remaining nineteen pass the strict numerical screen.

The paper replication also moves the block boundaries from approximately
one-third and two-thirds to one-quarter and three-quarters of the steps,
while keeping whole segments. It compares two versus three states again.
These are sensitivity analyses on the same animal, not independent biological
replications. The extended refit settings are in the manuscript's
`replication/compare-zebra-states.R` and `zebra-extra-starts.R`.

## See which steps change label

The intermediate state is partly a subdivision of the former short state.
To avoid counting every new name as a change, each three-state label is
mapped to the two-state label with which it shares the most steps. Several
new states may share the same parent. This mapping describes these fitted
sequences; it does not validate the labels against behaviour in the field.

```{r compare-labels}
changes <- compare_ssf_state_labels(comparison,
  from = "gamma::length_2", to = "gamma::length_3", threshold = .70)
changes$crosswalk
changes$mapping
```

The gamma models disagree on the parent label for `r sum(changes$steps$.changed)`
steps. Separately, `r sum(changes$steps$.ambiguous)` steps have a largest
smoothed probability below 0.70 in the three-state fit. This threshold helps
read the map; it is not a calibrated probability of classification error.

```{r map, fig.width=8, fig.height=7.7, fig.alt="The complete zebra track locates a 96-step window. Three detail panels show two-state labels, three-state labels, and changes in parent label or low assignment support."}
d <- changes$steps
# Use the 96-step window from the state-count analysis. It was chosen to
# show changes while including all three states, not as a representative sample.
window <- 4047:4142
colour_state <- c(Short = "#156d73", Intermediate = "#7a509a", Long = "#ab482b")
state_map <- function(field, title) {
  ggplot(d[window, ]) +
    geom_segment(aes(x0, y0, xend = x, yend = y, colour = .data[[field]]), linewidth = .7) +
    geom_point(aes(x, y, colour = .data[[field]]), size = 1) +
    geom_point(data = d[window[1L], ], aes(x0, y0),
      shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "#193541", size = 2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = colour_state, drop = TRUE) + coord_equal() +
    labs(title = title, x = "Relative easting (km)", y = "Relative northing (km)", colour = NULL)
}
overview <- plot(comparison, type = "track", from = "gamma::length_2", to = "gamma::length_3") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = min(d$x[window]) - .3, xmax = max(d$x[window]) + .3,
    ymin = min(d$y[window]) - .3, ymax = max(d$y[window]) + .3,
    fill = NA, colour = "#193541") +
  labs(title = "All 6,375 steps", subtitle = NULL,
    x = "Relative easting (km)", y = "Relative northing (km)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
change_map <- plot(comparison, type = "track",
  from = "gamma::length_2", to = "gamma::length_3", step_index = window) +
  labs(title = "Changes and assignment support", subtitle = NULL,
    x = "Relative easting (km)", y = "Relative northing (km)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))
(overview + state_map(".state_from", "Two states") +
    state_map(".state_to", "Three states") + change_map) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2) + plot_annotation(caption =
    "The box locates the same 96-step window. Uncertain means maximum smoothed probability below 0.70.")
```

These maps use the full-track fits. They show how interpretation changes
when we refit with a different number of states. The reserved-block scores
above address a different question about prediction.

## Add an environmental requirement

Suppose our long-step label should also require lower selection for woodland
than for grassland. We keep the length labels and add that requirement.
Grassland is the reference level, so the coefficient row is `habitatwoodland`.
The rule requires the upper end of its usual two-sided 95% Wald interval
to lie below zero in the long state.

```{r environmental-rule}
length_and_woodland <- ssf_taxonomy(
  "length_and_woodland", c("Short", "Intermediate", "Long"),
  formula = selection, order_by = "mean_step",
  rules = function(s) {
    upper <- ssf_contrast(s, "habitatwoodland", "Long")$upper
    c(
      length_ratio = s$metrics["Long", "mean_step"] >
        2 * s$metrics["Short", "mean_step"],
      lower_woodland_selection = upper < 0
    )
  }
)
fit3 <- comparison$fits[["gamma::length_3"]]
assessment <- assess_taxonomy(fit3, length_and_woodland, convention = "area")
assessment$checks
assessment$reasons
```

This rule concerns selection relative to available endpoints, conditional on
the model terms. It does not say every long step ends in grassland. Changing
only the taxonomy requires no refit and leaves the likelihood and predictive
scores unchanged. If the environmental variable were absent from the model,
we would need to add it to the formula and refit first. A variable constant
within every choice set cannot have a direct conditional selection effect.

This environmental rule was motivated by the fitted pattern, so we treat it
as an exploratory interpretation. In a confirmatory study, define the labels,
ordering and thresholds before inspecting the fitted states or reserved scores.
Missing standard errors make this interval rule return `NA`, which fails the
check. A failed rule is a reason to question the label, not to rename the
state silently.

## Make the ecological choice

For this track we retain three states for interpretation. Their full-track
fits pass the numerical and length-taxonomy checks, both families improve
held-out prediction, and their length profiles are similar. Four states may
predict better under the relaxed screen, but their parameter uncertainty is
not reliable here. This is a choice supported by these diagnostics, not proof
of a true biological state count. Independent activity observations or a
second animal would provide evidence that this comparison cannot supply.

For your own data, replace the formula, labels, ordering and rules in the
example. Keep the comparison blocks fixed across candidates, inspect missing
scores and failed checks, then look at the trajectory before attaching
behavioural names.

The track and vegetation grid come from [Bouderbala, Nicosia and Fortin
(2026)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0360547) and their
[Figshare archive, version 2](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34077912.v2).


## Add a between-state interval rule

The rule context contains joint covariance and a table identifying each
coefficient by its state label and term. This comparison uses the covariance
between the two persistence coefficients:

```{r contrast}
fit3 <- comparison$fits[["gamma::length_3"]]
a <- assess_taxonomy(fit3, taxonomies[[3]], "area")
ssf_contrast(a$context, "cos_angle", from = "Short", to = "Intermediate")
```

The estimate is Intermediate minus Short. An interval entirely above zero
would support an additional positive-difference rule, conditional on this
fitted model. Deciding to add that rule after seeing these results makes it
exploratory. It does not provide a significance test corrected for choosing
the state count, taxonomy or solution.

## Finish with ecological labels

The length labels make the comparison easy to read. We can go further by
requiring both a movement signature and an environmental association.
For illustration, we define local movement, grassland movement and
persistent grassland travel. The two longer states must select grassland
relative to each of the three other endpoint habitats. Each successive
state must have a mean step more than twice as long and greater directional
persistence, supported by a coefficient contrast.

This is an exploratory taxonomy suggested by the fitted pattern. It
illustrates how to write ecological requirements; it is not an independent
test of these behaviours. The factor `habitat` refers to the endpoint.
Grassland is its reference level.

```{r ecological-definition}
source(system.file("extdata", "zebra-ecological-taxonomy.R",
  package = "behavSSF", mustWork = TRUE))
zebra_ecological_taxonomy
```

```{r ecological-assessment}
ecology <- assess_taxonomy(fit3, zebra_ecological_taxonomy(), convention = "area")
ecology$checks
```

```{r ecological-effects, fig.width=12, fig.height=7.8, fig.alt="State-specific coefficient intervals for directional persistence, direction to a grassland target and three endpoint habitats compared with grassland."}
state_colours <- c("Local movement" = "#784B8B",
  "Grassland movement" = "#B6501C", "Persistent grassland travel" = "#166484")
effect_terms <- c("cos_angle", "cos_diff_theta_to_target",
  "habitatbushed grassland", "habitatbushland", "habitatwoodland")
effect_names <- c("Previous heading", "Direction to grassland target",
  "Bushed grassland vs grassland", "Bushland vs grassland", "Woodland vs grassland")
plot_ssf_states(fit3, panel = "coefficients", assessment = ecology,
  terms = effect_terms, term_labels = setNames(effect_names, effect_terms),
  colours = state_colours)
```

Negative habitat coefficients support greater selection for grassland
relative to that endpoint habitat, conditional on the other model terms.
The two longer states satisfy this requirement. The target-direction
intervals include zero. We therefore describe grassland selection, rather
than habitat-directed travelling. Selection of an endpoint habitat and
orientation towards a target fixed at the start of a step are different
quantities.

```{r ecological-habitat-overview, fig.width=13, fig.height=11, fig.alt="Ecological labels linked to a 48-hour trajectory, observed movements and directional persistence in the three-state habitat model."}
plot_ssf_states(fit3, assessment = ecology, step_scale = 1000, step_unit = "m",
  coord_unit = "km", segment = names(which.max(table(fit3$observations$ID))),
  step_range = c(1, 96), terms = "cos_angle", colours = state_colours)
```

The map tells us where the inferred states occur. The distributions describe
their movements. The coefficient intervals show which environmental and
directional claims the model supports. Reading them together makes the
state labels useful to an ecologist while keeping their limits visible.
